title: Dialogue, not debate
hook: Nanak listens and answers; he does not mock

segments.voice: Yesterday, humble before truth: the side that bows is the heavier one. Your line was the yogis bowed. Where did you let your pan sink? Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

A reply is half typed. The other person said something wrong, maybe a little smug, and there's a perfect line ready, the kind that would get laughs. The thumb hovers over send. Family dinners and group chats have moments like that. The Sidh Gosht has its own. The yogis come at Nanak with hard questions, some of them pointed: who are you, where do you come from, why did you leave home. He had every chance to score points. Today: dialogue, not debate.
screen: `A REPLY, HALF TYPED.` → `THE PERFECT CUTTING LINE.` → `HARD QUESTIONS ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Look first at the shape of the thing. Sidh Gosht means the discourse with the Siddhs, and it's written that way: they ask, he answers, back and forth, question after question. It isn't a speech with an audience. It's a conversation with people in it. Now look at how he answers. Over the past days we've met their words: earrings, the patched coat, the breath, the way of yoga. Nanak never throws those words back at them. He picks each one up, turns it in the light, and fills it with something new. True earrings, he says: the Guru's Word. The way of yoga: the Word lived in ordinary life. That's a respectful move. It takes the other person's language seriously enough to use it. Mockery does the opposite. It takes someone's words and holds them up to be laughed at. Guru Nanak has a short verse about this in the Asa di Var. In paraphrase: speak harsh, tasteless words, and body and mind turn harsh and tasteless too. The word he uses is phikka, flat, without savor, like food with no salt. A cutting reply might win the room, but in that verse it leaves the speaker poorer. So why does it matter on an ordinary Tuesday? Because a disagreement often offers the same fork: debate, where someone has to lose, or dialogue, where both people leave having been heard. The Sidh Gosht doesn't pretend the yogis and Nanak agreed on everything. It shows that strong disagreement and kindness can sit in the same circle.
screen: `THEY ASK, HE ANSWERS.` · `HE USES THEIR OWN WORDS.` · `PHIKKA: HARSH, WITHOUT SAVOR.` · `DISAGREE, AND STAY KIND.` · then, large: `ANSWER KINDLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer one question kindly. Sit, and bring to mind a question someone asked you recently that annoyed you. Maybe it was pointed. Maybe it was the third time they asked. Hear it again. Notice the quick, sharp answer that rises first, and just let it pass. Then look for the kind answer: honest, still your own view, but spoken so the other person could actually take it in. Rehearse it once in your mind. If you pray, you can ask for sweet speech. If you don't, simply let the sharp answer go. The bell holds the time.
Dialogue. The Sidh Gosht is built as a conversation: the yogis ask, Nanak answers, and he never mocks. Today's word.
Your line: answer kindly. Today, when the cutting reply is ready, use the other person's own words, and answer them with salt, not with bite. Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching values sweet speech, and the Sidh Gosht is read as a model of conversation with other seekers; it is recited in full in some Sikh homes and gurdwaras.

fork.setup: the yogis ask Nanak a pointed question about his path. what does he do?
options: take their words seriously and answer in them.
fork.reveal: he answers, using their own words, and fills them with the Guru's Word. no mockery anywhere.

original.note: gosht: discourse, conversation, as in the title Sidh Gosht.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dialogue is a polite debate with a winner.
what it means: the yogis ask, Nanak answers, and he takes their language seriously instead of mocking it.
what a scholar hears: gosht means discourse; the hymn is built from questions and answers, and Nanak refills the yogis' own terms.
